title: Speak and listen
brief: A voice arrives and must be answered before the caller loses patience. Latency, control over the text in between and cost are open. Choose the architecture, the transport and the turn detection.

blocks.text: Five ways to build a voice agent

blocks.md: OpenAI's voice guide says to start new conversational voice apps with **GPT-Live**: full duplex, so it listens while it speaks, with reasoning delegated to a separate backend, billed per second, over WebRTC, WebSocket or SIP [[r3]]. The Realtime API runs one speech-to-speech model per session. A chained pipeline (speech-to-text, agent, text-to-speech) is the choice when you must inspect text between stages. On Azure, **Voice Live** bundles recognition, model and synthesis [[r7]], and Foundry voice-based prompt agents add managed voice to a prompt agent and are preview as of 2026-10-13 [[r8]].

blocks.title: Voice architectures
blocks.intro: Product names and status were checked on 2026-10-13. Confirm availability on your cloud and region.

options.name: Chained pipeline
options.summary: Speech-to-text, then a text agent, then text-to-speech.
pros: Text between stages can be inspected, redacted and logged
cons: More parts to run and monitor
options.bestWhen: Compliance needs the text, or a tuned text agent already exists.
options.avoidWhen: The lowest latency is the top priority.

options.name: Realtime speech-to-speech
options.summary: One speech-to-speech model per session over browser WebRTC or server WebSocket.
pros: One model handles audio in and out
cons: The whole conversation is resent each turn, so later turns cost more
options.bestWhen: A new voice app where latency matters most.
options.avoidWhen: You must filter text before the model sees it.

options.name: GPT-Live with a backend
options.summary: Full duplex voice that delegates reasoning to a separate backend through Responses or client delegation.
pros: A slow backend does not freeze the conversation
Keeps an existing agent as the brain
Partner paths for LiveKit, Twilio, Telnyx, Daily and Pipecat
cons: Backend tokens are billed separately from per-second voice time
Documented on the OpenAI platform, so check Azure availability
options.bestWhen: Reasoning is slow or tool heavy and the voice must stay responsive.
options.avoidWhen: You need Azure-managed speech features and data zones.

options.name: Azure Voice Live
options.summary: Managed speech-to-speech with a WebSocket interface close to the Azure OpenAI Realtime events.
pros: Noise suppression, echo cancellation and end-of-turn detection
Over 140 speech-to-text locales and over 600 standard voices
cons: Less control over the text path
options.bestWhen: You want Azure Speech features without hosting orchestration.
options.avoidWhen: A GA-only rule covers the whole stack.

options.name: Foundry voice-based prompt agent
options.summary: Managed voice for a prompt agent, native speech-to-speech or cascaded.
pros: Cascaded mode adds model, voice and phrase-list control
cons: No direct SIP, and no standard Teams card layout
options.bestWhen: A prompt agent needs a voice front end and preview is allowed.
options.avoidWhen: Production needs a preview waiver you cannot get.

blocks.title: Pick a voice architecture
blocks.prompt: Change how much you must control the text, how strict latency is, whether a text agent exists and preview tolerance.

Reasoning sits in the voice model unless tools delegate.

strict.why: Full duplex keeps the call responsive.

blocks.takeaway: Speech-to-speech wins on latency, chained wins when text must be inspected, and GPT-Live wins when a slow brain must not freeze the call.

blocks.title: Audio tokens and history growth

vars.v: the full conversation is resent each turn, and prompt caching is best effort

blocks.example: A turn of 10 s user audio and 10 s assistant audio is 100 + 200 = **300** tokens. At turn 9 the resent history is 8 x 300 = **2,400** tokens before the new audio, so long calls cost more per turn. Changing history or instructions mid-session busts the cache.

items.symptom: The assistant cuts in when callers pause to think
items.cause: `server_vad` is silence based and cannot tell a thinking pause from a finished thought
items.fix: Use `semantic_vad` with a lower `eagerness`, or lengthen `silence_duration_ms`. Measure interruption rate.

items.symptom: Cost per call climbs on long calls
items.cause: The full conversation is resent each turn and mid-session edits bust the cache
items.fix: Keep instructions stable. `session.truncation.retention_ratio` defaults to 1.0, and 0.8 drops extra items so the cache stays valid longer [[r5]].

items.symptom: Calls drop at the one hour mark
items.cause: The Azure realtime session maximum is 60 minutes
items.fix: Build reconnect logic that carries state to a new session [[r6]].

items.cause: `gpt-live-transcribe` and `gpt-realtime-whisper` need turn detection omitted or `null` and a manual `input_audio_buffer.commit`

items.symptom: The 'one moment' filler arrives too late in a Foundry voice agent
items.fix: Lower it, as the docs advise [[r9]].

blocks.md: `session.audio.input.turn_detection` takes `server_vad` (silence based, the default, tunable with `threshold`, `prefix_padding_ms` and `silence_duration_ms`) or `semantic_vad` (a classifier on the words, with `eagerness` of `low`, `medium`, `high` or `auto`, where `auto` equals `medium`) [[r4]]. `create_response` and `interrupt_response` apply to conversations only. On Azure, `turn_detection` accepts `none`, `semantic_vad` or `server_vad` [[r6]].

items.title: Go deeper: Foundry voice agents and Voice Live

blocks.md: Foundry voice agents offer native speech-to-speech and cascaded architectures. Phone channels use Teams Phone extensibility and Twilio. Noise reduction values are `near_field`, `far_field` and `azure_deep_noise_suppression` [[r8]]. Voice Live models include `gpt-realtime-2.1` (also `-datazone` and `-regional`), `gpt-realtime-2.1-mini`, `gpt-realtime-1.5`, `gpt-realtime`, `gpt-realtime-mini`, `gpt-4o` and `gpt-4o-mini`. It adds avatars, phrase lists and custom voice [[r7]].

items.title: Go deeper: moving from the realtime beta to GA

blocks.md: Drop the `OpenAI-Beta: realtime=v1` header, mint keys with `/v1/realtime/client_secrets`, use `/v1/realtime/calls`, set `session.type` and use renamed events such as `response.output_audio.delta` [[r3]]. On Azure use the `/openai/v1` endpoint with no `api-version`. The Azure API does not connect straight to end-user devices, so a client integration must terminate the audio [[r6]].

quiz.q: Each turn has 10 s of user audio and 10 s of assistant audio. User audio costs 1 token per 100 ms and assistant audio 1 token per 50 ms. At the start of turn 9, how many audio tokens of history are resent, ignoring text and truncation?
quiz.hint: One turn is 100 + 200 tokens. Eight turns are complete.
quiz.explain: 10 s of user audio is 100 tokens and 10 s of assistant audio is 200 tokens, so a turn is 300 tokens. Eight completed turns give 8 x 300 = 2,400 tokens, resent before the new audio. This growth is why long calls cost more per turn.

quiz.q: Match each setting to what it does.

pairs.r: A classifier on the words, with `eagerness` low, medium, high or auto
Defaults to 1.0, and 0.8 keeps the cache valid longer

quiz.explain: Silence-based detection and word-aware detection are the two turn-detection modes. Transcription-only models need turn detection off and a manual commit. The retention ratio controls how much history truncation drops.

quiz.q: Compliance requires card numbers to be redacted from the transcript before any model sees it. Which architecture fits?
options: Native speech-to-speech, since it has the lowest latency
GPT-Live full duplex, since it listens while it speaks
A chained pipeline, so text can be inspected and redacted between stages
A Foundry voice agent in native mode, which is preview
quiz.explain: Only a chained pipeline exposes text between stages, so a redaction step can sit there. Native speech-to-speech and GPT-Live hand audio to the model, and native mode in a Foundry voice agent has the same property plus preview status.

quiz.q: Callers say the assistant cuts in while they pause to think. The session uses `server_vad` with defaults. Which change fits best?
options: Switch to `semantic_vad` with `eagerness` set to `low`, or lengthen `silence_duration_ms`
Lower the temperature of the voice model so the replies become shorter and less likely to interrupt
Disable turn detection and send audio as one long message
Move from WebRTC to WebSocket to cut latency
quiz.explain: Silence-based detection ends a turn on any long enough pause. A word-aware detector with low eagerness, or a longer silence window, waits longer. Temperature does not control turn endings, disabling detection removes the conversation loop, and a transport swap changes latency, not turn logic.

takeaways: Chained gives text control, speech-to-speech gives latency, GPT-Live keeps the call alive while a backend thinks
Silence-based turn detection cannot tell a thinking pause from a finished thought
Audio history is resent each turn, so long calls cost more per turn
Foundry voice agents are preview, and Azure realtime sessions end at 60 minutes
